01 · Full engine reverse engineering

Wasteland engine reverse engineering

Wasteland · Interplay, 1988 · 4 disk sides

The project covers the full engine and its data formats. It includes an EasyFlash port with persistent state and an editor for the original record format.

What the tooling produced

  • Annotated engine source: 7,226 lines. An API jump table at $0200–$04FF with 197 vectors is the interception surface for the cartridge backend.
  • Extraction verified in both directions: 197 directory entries, 0 missing, 0 orphans.
  • Cartridge port with a unified loader, per-file packing and a flash journal that keeps the world state across sessions.
  • An editor for areas, texts, portraits and quests, with a byte-exact serializer back to the game's format.

Findings

  • Portraits carry no colour data of their own. This follows from the renderer, the fixed window colour setup and the foe records, whose byte 7 selects the portrait. Result: all 88 portraits export with their names.
  • Text ids, items and paragraph triggers connect through the scene scripts. The editor derives a cross-area quest graph from item ids and keywords.
  • Verification: the text codec re-encodes all 42 records with 0 differences. The engine's own record routine returns identical results for 4,407 (group, id) pairs; after a cartridge boot, live RAM matches the repacked data in 9,206 of 9,206 bytes.

02 · Disk-to-EasyFlash conversion

Accolade Comics EasyFlash port

Accolade Comics · Accolade, 1987 · released 2026 on CSDb ↗

Six disk sides became one 1 MB EasyFlash image. The port replaces the sector-load routine at $1998. The remaining engine stays byte-exact.

What the tooling produced

  • Loader decoded: drive code uploaded to $0402, 2-byte key-addressed files, lookup-table pages; 728 unique files extracted.
  • Only the sector-load routine at $1998 is replaced; it serves bytes from cartridge banks. Dispatcher $0C23, scene table $0900, sector assembler $0D46 and the script bytecode VM stay byte-exact.
  • Protection checks are answered with a synthesised directory sector; save games are written to flash through EAPI.

Semantic annotation, same bytes

The disassembler supplies addresses and generated labels. Annotations add routine names, contracts, and callers. The routine below loads lookup pages, allocates memory, inserts a scene entry, and streams sectors through $1998.

03 · Behaviour-driven testing

Last Ninja engine migration tests

Last Ninja 1–3 · System 3 · unified engine

Three games are being merged into one data-driven engine. Tests run the original and replacement code with identical input, then compare the results.

Ongoing work

How behaviour is tested

  • Scenarios in Gherkin: given a real cartridge image, wait frames, hold the joystick, then read memory. Each run uses a private headless TRX64 machine.
  • Replay: the original routine and the new routine run on identical inputs — 833,814 wall tests for Last Ninja, 608,334 for Last Ninja 2. Pass means 0 differences.
  • Lock-step: the original game and the new engine run side by side with the same input and random seed and are compared at checkpoints.

Results

  • Last Ninja 2, level 6: the player walked off the roof in mid-air. Reading the converted level data predicted ignored edge handlers; lock-step confirmed the fall at x 54 via trigger 49. Replay differences went from 436 to 0.
  • Documentation said Last Ninja 2 wall lines are one-sided. The code tests the crossing from both sides, and the replay's 436 differences were all enemy steps blocked that way. Reading the code found 32 such claims that the code contradicts.
  • Status: collision, walls, falls, exits, sprites and hazards migrated with 0 differences. Combat, AI, items and boss logic are in progress.

Scenario steps run verbatim in the sandbox; the returned values are recorded under each step.

04 · A code graph for 6502 assembler

Neuromancer 6502 code graph

Neuromancer · Interplay, 1988 · engine, overlays and 1541 drive code

Static analysis produced 3,079 nodes and 11,889 edges. A separate human layer contains 1,634 annotated nodes. Re-analysis does not overwrite that layer.

What the graph answers

  • $7403 has exactly two writers: engine initialisation and the overlay itself. The readers are the demand-load test for the $7400 overlay slot, spread over two payloads.
  • Engine API routine $5292 draws a string from 32 call sites. The computed signature flags that it reads its own return address — proof that the string pointer is an inline word after each JSR, which a linear disassembly decodes as garbage.
  • Argument domains across call sites: the disk loader at $4BEC takes its sector from the tables at $FE3C and $6300, the ones the load-table documentation describes.

Impact before an edit

  • Changing the two-instruction banking helper $4B9F breaks 6 direct callers. Through its write to $01 it also reaches the raster IRQ and the fastloader in another file — no call edge connects them.
  • UNKNOWN is a separate result, never counted as low risk: indirect accesses, code on the 1541's own 6502, self-modifying writes.
  • For the EasyFlash port, "identified" is defined as graph predicates: byte coverage, a signature per routine, every indirect access resolved or declared.

Query output from the Neuromancer project graph, trimmed. Neuromancer © 1988 Interplay.

05 · VIC-20 cartridge to C64 port

Cosmic Cruncher C64 port

Cosmic Cruncher · Commodore, 1982 · VIC-20 8K cartridge · C64 port by TREX, 2026

The 8 KB cartridge was disassembled and rebuilt byte for byte. The game code runs unchanged on the C64; only its picture, colours, sound, joystick, keys and interrupts are carried over.

What the tooling produced

  • Annotated 64tass source of the cartridge ($A000–$BFFF) that rebuilds byte-identical, with memory, RAM and pointer reports.
  • A generated patch list: every changed byte in $A000–$BFFF sits at a listed site, 0 outside. Charset moved to $3800, the game's $00/$01 pointer moved to $FB/$FC, 11 IRQ vector pairs and 6 VIA reads redirected to C64 shims.
  • Two builds on one disk: the faithful version with the VIC-20 picture and speed, and a C64 version with hardware sprites. Both run on PAL and NTSC at the original's speed.
  • Trainer menu with five options, a high-score saver that refuses to save while an option is on, and a 10-page in-game manual.

Findings

  • The screen is at $1C00, not the $1E00 of an unexpanded VIC-20: the boot stores HIBASE $0288 = $1C before CINT. Reading the boot code refuted the assumption.
  • The game reads bonus_colour at $1046 before it ever writes it. A VIC-20 leaves non-zero power-up RAM there; the zero-filled port kept sprite characters on the top lane. The boot now stores $01, proven by a scenario.
  • Verification: 25 scenarios on the release build, 25 pass. Every file was read back off the D64 and matched the fresh build byte for byte.

Patch from the generated V1 patch list; scenario shortened (one Then line removed, comments added). Cosmic Cruncher © 1982 Commodore.

06 · Commodore 16 to C64 port

The Magician's Curse C64 port

The Magician's Curse · Gremlin Graphics, 1986 · Commodore 16 / Plus/4 · C64 port by TREX, 2026

The C16 game was depacked, disassembled and rebuilt byte for byte. The game image runs at its original addresses $0700–$3FFF; a port layer at $4000–$7FFF maps the TED chip to the VIC-II, SID and CIAs.

What the tooling produced

  • Annotated 64tass source: 5,466 lines for the game image, 416 for the block the game copies to $0200. The rebuild compares identical to the depacked original.
  • The port source includes that listing unchanged and overlays its patches. The byte diff against the original shows 66 changed runs in $0700–$3FFF, each listed in a patch register; no run contains a branch target except at its first byte.
  • Two builds: a faithful version with the C16 character graphics, and a C64 version in which the player, bats and apples are hardware sprites shown over a second playfield screen at $2800.
  • A release disk with both builds, trainer menus, a high-score file, an in-game manual, a solution and a printable map of all 48 rooms drawn from the game data.

Findings

  • Most TED writes need no patch: with the KERNAL banked out they land in RAM at $FF00–$FF3F, and the port reads border, colours and sound back from there. Patched: TED reads, interrupt control, and the display and border writes whose timing matters.
  • The 48-room tour found an NTSC hang in the sprite build: the room-change blank waited for raster line 256+, and on NTSC the status interrupt covered lines 256–262. The wait now counts that interrupt instead.
  • A web description credited another publisher and called the statue the end of the game. The title screen and inlay name Gremlin Graphics; the code adds a bonus and restarts one skill level higher.
  • Verification: 15 event checks pass; 48-room tours pass for both builds on PAL and NTSC. Four faster graphics routines return the same memory and registers as the originals in an isolated 6502 sandbox.

Excerpts from the annotated listing and the V1 port source; comments shortened. The Magician's Curse © 1986 Gremlin Graphics.
